prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: optical lattice clocks (B041) as a single-part prize for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Round 1 did not move my view of the physics, but it sharpened what the citation must say. The credited idea is the magic-wavelength lattice, in which the light shift of the trapping field cancels for the clock transition so that many atoms can be interrogated at once, Doppler- and recoil-free. That is a physical insight about atomic polarisabilities, and it is a different step from the frequency comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012). Katori proposed it and realised the first strontium lattice clocks; Ye's group brought the lattice clock to the 1e-18 regime and, through spin-polarised many-body clocks, exposed and controlled the systematics that limited it. Independent clocks agreeing below 1e-18 on different continents settle maturity without any reference to the SI second. The consequences are concrete: millimetre-scale redshift measurements, tighter limits on constants and ultralight dark matter. Six of eight members hold the same configuration with the same pair, and the objections raised concern weighting, not facts. I judge the credit more defensible than for any other shortlisted candidate. I regard that as scientific merit and not a head count, because a prize whose credited names are contestable has a weaker claim to say who did the work.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection stays the one I gave in round 1 and that Danielsson, Johansson, Pearce and Olsson sharpened: this is a measurement invention, and a third prize in precision spectroscopy after 2005 and 2012 may look incremental next to field-creating matter such as moire graphene. I answer it on the physics: the many-atom magic-wavelength regime is not a refinement of ion clocks, but I concede that the committee should decide openly whether it gives weight to novelty of this kind. The second weakness is credit. Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups made decisive contributions to individual milestones, and two names cannot cover them; Ye's credit also rests partly on his comb and broader clock programme, which the citation must not lean on. I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the experimental systematics, which lie outside my own field.

responses.point: The chair asks how much of Ye's credit rests on the lattice clock rather than on the comb and broader clock programme, and whether the citation should treat the 2005 prize only as enabling technology.
responses.response: I answer yes to the second question and would put it in the wording: the citation names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping, and mentions neither combs nor frequency metrology in general. On Ye, my reading of the record, which I cannot check independently, is that his group's lattice-clock accuracy and stability results and the many-body spin-polarised clock work are sufficient on their own, so I need nothing from his comb-based spectroscopy to justify the credit. If a member can show that his lattice-clock contribution cannot stand without the comb work, I would want that stated now, because it would change my view of the pair. I also accept your point that the missing SI redefinition is a reason some may wait, but I do not hold it myself: the evidence is already in hand.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice concept, not combs or ion traps, is the citable discovery, since the many-atom regime is covered by neither 2005 nor 2012, and that accuracy records by other groups refine rather than originate it.
responses.response: I agree and I rely on this argument, but I would add a limit to it. It works for Katori's origination and for the first strontium realisations; it is weaker as a defence of every later milestone, where the Paris, PTB and NIST groups carried real weight. The citation should therefore say invention and realisation, and the committee should not claim that two names capture the clock field. Your Boulder disclosure does not change my view of your argument, since you reached the same conclusion as colleagues with no such tie, and I see no need for recusal on B041.

responses.point: Olsson judges that the field-creating novelty of twisted bilayer graphene outweighs the cleaner allocation of B041, while admitting she cannot claim B017 is the safer prize.
responses.response: This is the real disagreement and I think it is a fair one. I agree that moire quantum materials opened a new class of correlated matter and that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by decisive experiments is the structure a prize should reward. I still put it behind the clock for three reasons that bear on the science: the origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, sample-to-sample variation is large, and Cao, Fatemi and earlier twisted-bilayer theory fall outside any three-name credit that I can make convincing. In round 1 I said I would not oppose B017 if the committee rewards the platform rather than the mechanism; I keep that, and I would still list it as my first alternative. But I would not call it mature enough to outrank the clock this year.

responses.point: Eriksson would build a B017 citation on the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated phases rather than on a mechanism, and says he would accept B041 if the committee judges maturity decisive.
responses.response: Building the citation on the prediction and the observed phases is the right way to handle the mechanism, and it answers part of my concern, because existence of the phases is well reproduced. It does not answer the credit problem you yourself acknowledge: Cao and Fatemi did the 2018 measurements, and a citation cannot name them without breaking the three-person limit. That asymmetry is why I treat B017 as an alternative. Your willingness to accept B041 on maturity grounds is useful; I would add that my reason is credit and settled interpretation together, not maturity alone.

responses.point: Lindroth first raised the question of tying a clock prize to the SI redefinition and notes that other lattice-clock pioneers, especially the Paris and NIST groups, cannot be weighed from the supplied credit alone.
responses.response: You are better placed than I am to say whether Katori and Ye are complete for the lattice concept, and I note that you, having raised the redefinition, now say that the evidence base is already sufficient and that prize timing is not hurt by waiting. I read that as removing the SI objection. On the Paris and NIST groups, we agree that a two-name prize leaves out real contributors. My answer is that the Nobel citation rewards the originating concept and decisive demonstration, and a narrowly drawn citation is more defensible than a broader one that would need a third name at the cost of Ye or Katori.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that a diffuse PeV neutrino flux is a fact about nature that no theory predicted in detail, and that IceCube's lower maturity of source identification does not make the physical result shallow.
responses.response: I accept that correction. I called the physical result less deep than the instrument, which was too strong: the diffuse flux is established and the question of where cosmic rays are accelerated is deep. My remaining difficulty with B029 is credit and source maturity, and your own concession that no principled cut of a 300-plus collaboration exists is the reason it is not my preference. I would not exclude it in a later year once KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD sharpen the source population.

responses.point: Johansson asks that the invention-versus-discovery distinction not be applied asymmetrically, since the prize explicitly covers inventions and the clocks have produced physics results.
responses.response: I agree with this and it answers the question the chair posed about whether to apply the distinction at all. The statutes cover inventions and discoveries; earlier prizes in this area were for inventions. My earlier hesitation was about whether the committee wants to say so openly, not about whether it is permitted. The clocks have yielded physics results, in redshift over millimetres and in limits on constants, so the distinction does not bar B041, though it does explain why B017 and B029 keep claim to be more field-creating or deeper as discoveries.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's credit for the lattice clock is sufficient without his comb-based spectroscopy, and whether Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley or the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups have a claim comparable to Katori's or Ye's; I rely on colleagues and on the supplied credit, and cannot verify priority details myself.
Whether the committee will accept a third prize in precision spectroscopy and clocks after 2005 and 2012, given that it is a measurement invention.

For B003, priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Gallavotti, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert is unresolved and nobody but me has ranked it; I now treat it as a distant alternative rather than a configuration I would defend.
My recollection that the 2025 prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is unverified.
statement.conflict_note: No change: my documented co-authors and institutional ties (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg) do not include Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero. My work on stochastic physics is close in subject to B003, which I list as an alternative, but I know of no personal tie to Jarzynski, Evans, Crooks or Seifert. I have read Kroll's disclosure of the Boulder stay and Johansson's recusal on B028, and see no need for recusal on B041 or B017.
